overview: Fraserburgh beach curves for around three miles east of the town towards the Waters of Philorth local nature reserve. It's a town beach in the true sense: the harbour, shops and car parks are right behind it, so it's an easy place to surf without a long walk in.

At the town end stands Kinnaird Head, where a castle built from 1570 by Sir Alexander Fraser was converted into Scotland's first mainland lighthouse, first lit in 1787. The original lighthouse is now part of the Museum of Scottish Lighthouses, with lenses from lights all around the Scottish coast.

For surfing there are two different breaks. The open beach has lefts and rights spread along the sand, while a left-hand point works off the harbour end over rock. Surf-forecast calls the spot fairly consistent and usually uncrowded, though it's exposed and takes the full force of the weather.

text: Surf-forecast gives a northerly swell as best, with light southerly winds offshore. It works through all stages of the tide on the beach, and takes both groundswell and wind swell. The harbour-end point is more sensitive to the tide and the rocks, so watch it before paddling out.
Winter and spring are the strongest seasons, with June the most often clean month. The guide's warning is short: take care of rips and rocks.

Fraserburgh has a beach break with lefts and rights plus a left-hand point. North swell with a southerly offshore is the best match, and it's good at all stages of the tide. Take care of rips and rocks. It's unlikely to be crowded even when it's up. Winter and spring are best.
